Dear Administrator Oz:
North Olympic Healthcare Network (NOHN)â€™s mission is to provide patient-centered, 
quality driven, whole person healthcare services, accessible to everyone in our community.  
We are committed to providing family medicine, obstetric care, pharmacy services, behavior 
health, vision, and dental care.
CHCs are the healthcare home for many of Americaâ€™s medically underserved communities. 
NOHN serves a diverse and underserved patient population across Clallam County and 
surrounding areas, with strong focus on accessibility and affordability. We have over 19,000 
unique patients. For these patients, delays associated with prior authorization (PA) requirements 
can interrupt treatment, delay necessary care, and create significant barriers to maintaining stable 
health outcomes. These delays are common under the current system. A survey from the American 
Medical Association (AMA) found that 94 percent of physicians reported prior authorization 
delays patient care, while patient surveys found the average wait time for a prior authorization

administrative burden on CHCs already operating under significant workforce and financial 
constraints. NOHN therefore supports many of the changes in this proposed rule because of their 
potential to reduce administrative burden and improve timely patient access to medically necessary 
care and prescription drugs.

NOHN appreciates the opportunity to comment on the 2026 Interoperability Standards and Prior 
Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule. Our comments are broken into seven sections:
I.
Interoperability Standards for Application Programming Interfaces (APIs)
NOHN appreciates CMSâ€™ continued efforts to modernize interoperability infrastructure and 
improve electronic prior authorization (ePA) processes. We strongly support the goal of 
creating more standardized, interoperable, and real-time data exchange across payers, providers, 
and health IT systems to improve patient access to timely care. For CHCs, which frequently 
coordinate across multiple health plan issuers, hospitals, specialists, pharmacists, and behavioral 
health providers, the current PA environment remains highly fragmented and administratively 
burdensome. These proposals to standardize API functionality and data exchange requirements 
could significantly reduce duplicative documentation requests, improve visibility into PA 
requirements, and streamline care coordination for medically underserved patients. These reforms 
are urgently needed, given the scale of PA activity nationally. Reports show that Medicare 
Advantage (MA) Organizations made nearly 53 million PA determinations in 2024 alone, 
including more than four million full or partial denials.2 Similarly, a Medical Group Management 
Association (MGMA) report that physician practices continue to experience substantial staffing 
and workflow burden associated with manual PA processes, contributing to treatment delays and 
administrative strain across the healthcare system.3
These burdens are particularly significant for CHCs because of the unique patient populations they 
serve and the financial constraints under which they operate. CHCs serve more than 16 million 
Medicaid beneficiaries, over 6 million uninsured individuals, 20.5 million low-income individuals, 
1.1 million agricultural workers, and over 1.5 million homeless individuals.4 Additionally, more 
than 90 percent of CHCâ€™s patients have incomes below 200 percent of the federal poverty level 
(FPL), and many patients experience significant barriers related to transportation, broadband 
access, language services, and specialist availability.5 Delays caused by fragmented PA processes 
can disproportionately affect CHC patients, who cannot afford delays in medication access, 
specialty referrals, diagnostic testing, or behavioral health treatment. For providers operating with 
limited staffing and infrastructure capacity, repeated manual prioritization submissions, varying 
payer requirements, and inconsistent documentation standards divert essential resources away 
from direct patient care and essential services.

Concurrently, NOHN urges CMS to recognize that the success of these proposals will depend 
heavily on vendor readiness, operational consistency, and meaningful implementation 
support for safety-net providers. CHCs often lack the financial flexibility or internal IT 
workforce necessary to rapidly adapt to evolving interoperability requirements and frequently rely 
on a limited number of EHR vendors and/or third-party technology partners. Our small IT 
department and Pharmacy team cannot handle the current workload on PAs. The proposed rule 
appropriately places obligations for API readiness and interoperability on impacted payers. 
However, absent corresponding readiness requirements for vendors, we are concerned that CHCs 
may face compliance gaps and operational disruption despite acting in good faith. CMS should 
clarify that providers will not be penalized for failures attributable to vendors, 
clearinghouses, or EHR systems outside provider control. NOHN further recommends that 
CMS coordinate implementation timelines closely with the Office of the National Coordinator for 
Health IT (ONC) certification requirements and establish readiness validation or testing before 
enforcement begins. Inconsistent implementation of APIs and varying rollout schedules across 
payers could undermine the efficiencies CMS seeks to create in this proposed rule.6 
CMS should also consider establishing uniform minimum implementation requirements 
across Medicaid Managed Care Organizations (MCOs) and Qualified Health Plan (QHP) issuers, 
including standardized PA data fields, synchronized implementation guide (IG) timelines, and 
clearer operational standards. Without greater alignment across payers, CHCs may face 
fragmented payer-to-payer workflows that increase administrative complexity, create operational 
confusion, and undermine the efficiencies these reforms are intended to accomplish. 
NOHN is also concerned that the expansion of API-based exchange and ePA requirements 
may significantly increase cybersecurity exposure for CHCs, which are operating with a 
constrained workforce and infrastructure resources. The proposed rule contemplates a broad 
expansion of interoperable exchanges involving sensitive patient information, yet many CHCs, 
particularly those serving rural communities, lack dedicated cybersecurity teams or advanced IT 
infrastructure comparable to those of large health systems. While CHCs maintain a dedicated staff, 
these IT teams are small and usually wear multiple hats, meaning CHCs rely on third-party vendors 
and organizations to assist them in maintaining HIPAA compliance and securing their data. 
NOHN currently is limited to an IT department of two (budgeted for four) team members 
supporting three clinic sites, two pharmacies, and administration building. As interoperability 
requirements expand, CMS must ensure that CHCs are not absorbing unfunded costs associated 
with cybersecurity compliance, vendor upgrades, API integration, or ongoing maintenance 
requirements. To ensure CHCs can safely operationalize these changes without compromising 
patient access or continuity of care, CMS should provide technical assistance implementation 
guidance, cybersecurity and IT workforce development support, and dedicated health IT funding 
6 https://www.crowell.com/en/insights/client-alerts/cms-seeks-to-expand-interoperability-requirements-to-drug-pre-
authorization-faq

opportunities. CMS should also ensure that the final implementation framework reflects the 
operational realities and resource constraints under which CHCs deliver care to medically 
underserved communities.
Ultimately, NOHN supports CMSâ€™ broader interoperability goals because standardized, 
timely, and transparent data exchange can improve patient access to care and reduce 
administrative barriers that interfere with essential treatment. However, successful 
implementation will require CMS to pair these requirements with realistic timelines, coordinated 
national standards, robust vendor accountability, and targeted support for safety-net providers. 
With stronger implementation safeguards and implementation support, CMS can ensure these 
reforms improve care coordination and reduce administrative burden while protecting access to 
care for CHC patients. 
II.
Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs
NOHN supports CMSâ€™ proposal to establish ePA requirements for prescription drugs. We 
greatly appreciate the agencyâ€™s effort to extend interoperability reforms to medication access 
workflows. NOHN believes these proposals could meaningfully improve timely patient access to 
essential medications while reducing the administrative burden associated with manual PA 
processes. For CHCs, these changes could also improve point-of-prescribing visibility into 
formulary requirements, utilization management criteria, and authorization status, helping 
providers make more informed prescribing decisions during the patient encounter and reducing 
avoidable treatment delays associated with incomplete or inaccurate submissions.
The proposal to require all impacted payers to support ePA for every drug requiring PA is 
particularly important for CHCs. In community health, medication adherence is vital for managing 
chronic diseases, preventing costly hospitalizations, and improving overall quality of life.7 As 
previously mentioned, CHCs serve 3.5 million patients with diabetes, 6.2 million patients with 
hypertension, 10 million overweight or obese patients, and 3.2 million people with depression and 
other mood disorders.8 Compared to other many other clinics in WA state, NOHN serves an 
even older, poorer, sicker and more isolated population. This patient population is also more 
likely to experience non-clinical factors of health that can make timely medication access critical 
for avoiding preventable complications and maintaining continuity of care. NOHN has 
consistently advocated for improved ePA requirements to support operational efficiency and 
reduce administrative burden when implemented consistently and supported by interoperable 
technology infrastructure.9 Streamlined ePA workflows would reduce treatment interruptions,

At the same time, NOHN urges CMS to address several operational concerns with the proposed 
prescription drug ePA workflows. NOHN recommends that CMS require payers to expose 
benefit classification information through the Provider Access APIs (via the CRD Coverage 
Information extension) so providers can determine in real time whether a drug falls under 
the medical benefit or pharmacy benefit pathway. We have concerns that CHCs may face a 
significant burden in managing dual workflows across medical and pharmacy benefit pathways. 
Determining whether a medication falls under the medical benefit or pharmacy benefit may not 
always be clear in real time, particularly for drugs that may be clinic administered. NOHN also 
requests clarification on how PA determinations would apply in situations where a drug is 
covered under both medical and pharmacy benefits. Specifically, CMS should clarify whether 
a PA approval issued under one benefit pathway would also apply to the alternate payment 
pathway or whether separate authorization determinations would be required. For example, 
extended-release buprenorphine may be billed under the pharmacy benefit when dispensed through 
a pharmacy but under the medical benefit when administered in-clinic by a provider.10 Greater 
transparency in benefit classification could improve prescribing efficiency, reduce inappropriate 
denials, and support more accurate claims processing across payer systems. Medications such as 
GLP1, Buprenorphine, Adderall, diabetic supplies such as Dexcom, Lidocaine patches, and etc are 
highly impacted.
NOHN further requests that CMS carefully evaluate how these requirements will interact 
with pharmacy operations, including 340B contract pharmacy arrangements utilized by 
more than 65 percent of CHCs.11 As 340B covered entities, CHCs utilize 340B savings to help 
stretch limited resources to provide affordable medications and expanded services for medically 
underserved patients. Implementation of prescription drug ePA requirements will not occur in a 
single system. It will require coordination across entity-owned dispensing operations, contract 
pharmacies, third-party administrators (TPAs), EHR systems, pharmacy management systems 
(PMS), and payer APIs. That coordination can be difficult because PMS and EHR systems may 
not always be fully interoperable or able to exchange complete, structured information in real time. 
Our pharmacy software system Liberty does not communicate with EPIC and Cover My Meds 
(PAs platform).  Pharmacy interoperability stakeholders have identified persistent barriers, 
including limited EHR integration, difficulty incorporating native FHIR content, terminology, and 
value-set misalignment, limitations in medication data standards, and competing vendor 
priorities.12 Studies similarly show that pharmacy access to EHR data can improve clinical

III.
Improving Communications and Decision Timeframes for PA
NOHN appreciates the agencyâ€™s focus on greater transparency and timeliness and supports 
CMSâ€™ proposals to improve communication and align decision timelines for PAs. 
Standardized decision timeframes across payers and clearer communication requirements are 
critically important for the medically underserved patients CHCs serve. NOHN is particularly 
supportive of CMSâ€™ efforts to align PA timelines across all payers impacted by this rule by 
requiring more consistent response timeframes for both standard and expedited requests. 
Specifically, NOHN supports the proposed requirements that PA decisions for covered outpatient 
drugs be made no later than 24 hours after receipt of a request, that standard PA requests for items 
and services be addressed within 7 days, and that expedited requests be addressed within 72 hours. 
NOHN also supports CMSâ€™ proposal requiring QHP issuers on the FFEs to provide notice of PA 
decisions no later than 72 hours for standard requests and 24 hours for expedited requests for 
prescription drugs. These more uniform and expedited timelines will help reduce unnecessary 
delays in medication access and treatment initiation for patients with urgent or ongoing healthcare 
needs.
Delays in PA approvals frequently result in delayed treatment, interrupted medication access, and 
avoidable worsening of health conditions. Our Chief Medical Officer was reduced to tears 
recently over her frustration in attempting to obtain PA approval for a life-saving medication 
for a patient. The patient has autoimmune lung disease and inflammatory arthritis; both 
previously well controlled for 10 years with a twice-yearly infusion. Attempting to meet new 
PA requirements for that medication required over 4 hours of the doctorâ€™s time, over 20 
hours of staff time, and a 3-month delay in this patientâ€™s infusion. We are waiting to see 
whether the delay triggers a flare in her conditions, either of which could be life-altering.   
For CHCs serving medically underserved populations that already face non-clinical factors of 
health, these delays can have serious consequences. NOHN supports aligning PA timelines across 
programs to improve efficiency and accountability.
NOHN supports CMSâ€™ proposal to require payers to provide specific denial reasons for all 
drug PA denials, regardless of submission method. We believe this change will allow CHCs to

more efficiently correct incomplete submissions, pursue appeals, and resubmit requests without

NOHN also supports CMSâ€™ efforts to improve public reporting of PA denials and timeframes. 
This change is a step towards greater transparency that will improve payer accountability and

automatic approval for PA requests that are not decided within the required timeframes. We

IV.
Reporting Payer API Endpoints and Associated Information for CMS To Publish
NOHN supports CMSâ€™ proposal to require impacted payers to report API endpoints and 
associated information for publication on CMSâ€™ website. Having easy access to API endpoints 
9
in a centralized location fully operationalizes CMSâ€™ interoperability efforts. Currently, a provider 
must look up each payerâ€™s API endpoints individually to use the Prior Authorization API (PA API) 
to submit a PA request or the Provider Access API to request patient data, which can be incredibly 
burdensome. Having all impacted payersâ€™ API endpoints in one place will increase transparency, 
reduce provider burden, and improve the functionality of the reported API endpoints.
CHCs often have small IT departments that lack the capacity to manually search each payerâ€™s 
website for API endpoint information. The CHC IT departmentâ€™s limited resources could be better 
spent on strengthening and developing innovative technology solutions that benefit patients, such 
as cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and telehealth. App developers and EHR vendors also stand 
to benefit from centralized, easy access to these endpoints, improvements that also directly impact 
patient care, particularly given that EHR disruptions currently occur when hard-coded endpoints 
become outdated.
NOHN applauds CMS for the proposed timelines requiring payers to report API endpoint 
information. Existing impacted payers have until 60 days after the effective date of a final rule, 
while new impacted payers have until 60 days before they begin covering patients under the 
applicable CMS program. This approach strikes a reasonable balance between payer accountability 
and operational feasibility. We also support the proposal requiring impacted payers to update the 
information within one week of any changes and verify that the reported information is updated at 
least annually. CHC patients strongly benefit when CHC and its vendors have this up-to-date 
information, as incorrect information can delay access to and delivery of care. NOHN commends 
CMSâ€™ commitment to transparency and encourages the agency to publish API endpoint 
information on its website as machine-readable files. This will help maximize the utility and 
usability of this data. A machine-readable file prevents diverting valuable staff time to the 
interpretation of large amounts of data. As CMS considers the best approach for reporting and 
disseminating this information, we urge the agency to prioritize ease of access for primary care 
providers in safety net settings, especially those in rural areas with limited resources, while 
minimizing duplication and unnecessary complexity.
V.
Updates to Patient Access, Provider Directory, Provider Access, and Payer-to-
Payer APIs; API Usage Metrics
Information about PA for Drugs in the Patient Access, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs
NOHN supports CMS' proposal requiring impacted payers to make detailed information 
about PA requests and decisions for all drugs available through the Patient Access, Provider 
Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs beginning October 1, 2027. As discussed, PA for drugs 
remains a significant barrier to patients receiving timely care. Having information on APIs helps 
identify opportunities to improve them and monitor overall usage trends for key features. While 
we appreciate payersâ€™ independent efforts to improve transparency around PA, we applaud CMS 
10
for requiring metrics that will hold payers formally accountable. We encourage CMS to continue 
publishing trends in this data and to seek additional policy levers to ensure PAs are not 
inappropriate barriers to care for patients who need it.
NOHN appreciates the proposed timeframe for having PA information available through 
the APIs no later than one business day after the payer receives the request. This change 
aligns timeframes with the current policy for non-drug PAs. We also strongly support the 
requirement that PA information remain accessible for at least one year after the last status update. 
This is particularly critical for the populations CHCs serve. In 2024, CHCs provided care to over 
1.5 million homeless individuals and more than 1.1 million agricultural workersâ€”populations that 
move frequently and may not return to a CHC for months at a time.20 These patients have a limited 
window of engagement, making it difficult to track outstanding PA requests across care episodes. 
Retaining this information for an extended period supports continuity of care and ensures that 
future providers, accessing patient information through the Provider Access API, can quickly 
understand a patient's PA history and better meet their needs.
New Proposed Reporting Levels and Deadlines for API Usage Metrics
NOHN supports the proposal requiring Medicaid managed care plans and CHIP managed 
care entities to report Patient Access API usage metrics both by program and by plan. This 
added granularity will give CMS a clearer picture of where access gaps exist and how to target 
improvement efforts. Medicaid patients represent nearly half of CHC patients,21 and nearly 78 
percent of all Medicaid patients in the U.S. are in a managed care plan.22 NOHN in and of itself 
has approximately 4,000 patients in Medicaid managed care and or CHIP. Having 
disaggregated data helps improve the value of the reported data. Additionally, NOHN supports 
CMSâ€™ proposal to align deadlines with reporting periods. Better alignment reduces administrative 
confusion and makes data more meaningful.
NOHN also supports expanding the metrics that impacted payers must report for Provider 
Access, Payer-to-Payer, and PA APIs. Requiring payers to report denial rates, timeframes for 
extensions, and adjudicated appeals for both standard and expedited PAs will meaningfully 
improve transparency and accountability across the system. Beyond the suggested metrics, 
NOHN recommends that CMS also require measures of API functionality and usability. 
Although terabytes of health data are transmitted daily, much of it goes unused in practice because 
it is not surfaced directly to users or cannot be incorporated into clinical workflows. NOHN 
therefore recommends that CMS track the rate of successful API requests, as well as those rejected 
due to authorization failures or malformed queries, and instances where API calls were not 
received by the requester. Additionally, metrics such as structured versus unstructured data in the

Removing Drug Formulary Information from Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs
NOHN encourages CMS to reconsider its proposal to remove drug formulary information 
from the Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs. While CMS suggests that providers already 
have sufficient access to formulary information through payer websites and standard 
communications, this access is neither reliable nor real-time. As Pharmacy Benefit Managers 
(PBMs) increasingly expand the number of drugs excluded from formularies, formulary lists can 
change rapidly, meaning the information available on a payer's website may not reflect a patient's 
current coverage at the point of care. For CHC providers, who often serve patients covered by 
multiple different payers and lack the administrative infrastructure to conduct manual lookups 
across each, this gap is especially consequential. A provider who cannot quickly determine 
whether a drug is covered, or identify a covered alternative, may delay prescribing or default to a 
less optimal option. Retaining formulary information in the Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer 
APIs would reduce this lookup burden, support better prescribing decisions, and advance the 
transparency goals CMS has articulated throughout this rule. NOHN urges CMS to weigh this 
real-world impact on safety-net providers against the administrative burden it cites as justification 
for removal.
Federal Matching Funds
We appreciate the possibility that States operating Medicaid and CHIP programs might be 
able to access federal matching funds to support the new proposals. NOHN continues to 
request that CMS ensure safety-net providers are prioritized for these funds, if they are available. 
Safety-net providers, like CHCs, operate on thin margins and would greatly benefit from additional 
funding to help reduce costs such as provider training and implementation expenses. Many CHCs 
are currently under financial strain, with nearly half of CHCs operating with fewer than 90 days 
of cash on hand. The sector's average operating margin has turned negative; one in four reporting 
negative five percent (-5%) operating margins. In response to the unique needs of their patients, 
CHCs invest significant resources into training their staff and patients to meet meaningful use and 
interoperability requirements. CMS should consider the specific investments CHCs make, 
including costs, administrative setup, staff, training, clinical training, and patient education needs, 
and ensure appropriate interoperability and access.
VI.
Modifications to HIPAA Standards Related to PA
12
NOHN recommends that CMS provide transition support to safety-net providers, such as 
CHCs, during the transition from X12 to FHIR. We appreciate and support CMSâ€™ efforts to 
move away from X12, a legacy system, and towards FHIR standards, an important step in 
enhancing interoperability. However, CHCs and their clearinghouses will need to support both 
standards simultaneously during transition: X12 6020 for claims attachments (CMS-0053-F, 
compliance May 2028) and FHIR/CDex for PA attachments (CMS-0062-P, compliance in 2029). 
This dual-standard burden is real and must be acknowledged. As previously mentioned in this 
letter, CHCs have limited IT staff due to constrained budgets so CMS support would help 
immensely in the transition. Ultimately, NOHN requests that CMS extend its February 28, 
2024, National Standards Group enforcement discretion (FHIR PA API as X12 278 
substitute) to cover the CMS-0062-P transition period.23 This would provide relief for HIPAA-
covered entities to use a FHIR-based PA API in place of the older X12 278 standard without facing 
HIPAA Administrative Simplification enforcement penalties.
NOHN supports the use of Clinical Data Exchange (CDex) for PA attachments but 
recommends specific guardrails to reduce provider burden and enhance transparency. CDex 
allows payers to specify exactly what data they need and supports multiple formats (C-CDA, PDF, 
text, FHIR resources). However, CDex also creates a mechanism for payers to issue iterative, 
escalating data requests. NOHN recommends CMS:

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** North Olympic Healthcare Network (NOHN); signed by Beau J. Brown.
- **Stakeholder type:** Healthcare Provider; safety-net community health center.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** NOHN provides family medicine, obstetric care, pharmacy services, behavioral health, vision, and dental care to more than 19,000 patients in Clallam County and surrounding areas, including diverse and underserved populations.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

NOHN supports CMS's interoperability and drug electronic prior authorization proposals because they could reduce administrative burden and improve medication access for community health center patients. The organization urges CMS to pair these requirements with realistic timelines, vendor accountability, cybersecurity and funding support, benefit-pathway clarity, proactive PA expiration alerts, gold-carding and PA reduction, centralized endpoint and metrics publication, HIPAA transition support, and CMS/ONC harmonization.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; API-USAGE-METRICS; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** 45 CFR 170.315(g)(31)-(g)(33); CMS-0053-F; CMS-0062-P; HTI-4, 90 FR 37130; February 28, 2024 National Standards Group enforcement discretion; WISeR model references. The comment does not cite the proposed PA CFR sections in detail.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR; CRD/DTR/PAS HL7 Da Vinci IGs v2.2; CRD Coverage Information extension; Provider Access API; Patient Access API; Provider Directory API; Payer-to-Payer API; Prior Authorization API; CDex; C-CDA; PDF/text/FHIR resource attachments; X12 278; X12 6020 claims attachments; HIPAA standard transactions; ONC certification criteria.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Interoperability standards and API implementation support**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE
- **Position:** Support with modifications
- **Rationale:** Standardized APIs and ePA can reduce duplicative documentation and improve PA visibility, but CHCs have limited IT staff, vendor dependence, and cybersecurity constraints.
- **Specific request:** CMS should provide realistic timelines, vendor accountability, readiness validation/testing, ONC coordination, cybersecurity support, technical assistance, and funding for safety-net providers.

**Topic 2: Prescription drug ePA and benefit-pathway clarity**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support with clarification
- **Rationale:** ePA can improve point-of-prescribing access to formulary and PA information, but dual medical/pharmacy benefit workflows are burdensome and sometimes unclear for clinic-administered or specialty drugs.
- **Specific request:** CMS should require benefit classification through Provider Access APIs using the CRD Coverage Information extension and clarify whether approval under one benefit pathway applies to the alternate pathway.

**Topic 3: Pharmacy operations and 340B coordination**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** CHC pharmacy operations involve entity-owned pharmacies, contract pharmacies, TPAs, EHRs, pharmacy management systems, payer APIs, and 340B accumulation data that may not interoperate in real time.
- **Specific request:** CMS should coordinate with the Office of Pharmacy Affairs and provide technical assistance, implementation guidance, and funding support for CHCs.

**Topic 4: PA expiration alerts and PA reduction**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** ePA alone may accelerate an inefficient process and may increase PA volume unless paired with reform; lack of expiration notice causes treatment interruptions.
- **Specific request:** CMS should mandate proactive FHIR-based PA expiration alerts, extend gold-carding to prescription drugs, and sunset PA categories with consistently high approval rates.

**Topic 5: Decision timeframes, denial reasons, and automatic approval**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support with stronger enforcement
- **Rationale:** Uniform decision timeframes and specific denial reasons help CHCs correct submissions, appeal, and avoid back-and-forth delays; payer delays can interrupt life-sustaining treatment.
- **Specific request:** CMS should finalize aligned timelines, require actionable denial notices, expand reporting, strengthen oversight, and deem PA requests approved if payers miss required deadlines.

**Topic 6: Public API endpoint reporting**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** CHCs lack capacity to manually locate each payer's API endpoints, and outdated hard-coded endpoints disrupt EHR workflows.
- **Specific request:** CMS should publish payer API endpoint information centrally on its website in machine-readable form, require one-week updates after changes, and prioritize usability for safety-net and rural primary care providers.

**Topic 7: API usage metrics and PA data availability**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support with expansion
- **Rationale:** Program- and plan-level usage metrics, denial rates, timeframes, appeals, and API functionality indicators would improve accountability and identify access gaps.
- **Specific request:** CMS should report successful and failed API requests, authorization failures, malformed queries, unreceived calls, structured versus unstructured responses, workflow impact, calls per query, queries per user, and API maintenance costs.

**Topic 8: Formulary information in APIs**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS; GENERAL
- **Position:** Oppose removal
- **Rationale:** Payer websites and standard communications do not provide reliable real-time formulary access for CHCs serving patients across many plans.
- **Specific request:** CMS should retain drug formulary information in Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs.

**Topic 9: HIPAA PA standards transition**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Support with transition support
- **Rationale:** Moving from X12 to FHIR can enhance interoperability, but CHCs and clearinghouses may need to support X12 6020 and FHIR/CDex simultaneously.
- **Specific request:** CMS should provide transition support and extend National Standards Group enforcement discretion allowing the FHIR PA API as an X12 278 substitute through the CMS-0062-P transition period.

**Topic 10: CDex guardrails**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** CDex can clarify payer documentation needs but also could enable iterative, escalating requests.
- **Specific request:** CMS should require payers to request all needed documentation initially, limit solicited attachment requests to two per PA transaction, and set maximum payer response timeframes after CDex attachments are received.

**Topic 11: ONC harmonization and certification timing**
- **Provision ID:** ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** CMS payer deadlines may precede certified provider-facing technology availability, and HTI-5 changes could weaken supporting infrastructure needed by CHCs.
- **Specific request:** CMS and ONC should issue joint implementation guidance and publish a harmonization assessment before the CMS-0062-P final rule; providers should not be penalized for unavailable certified technology.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1:** NOHN supports mandatory and standardized API/ePA functionality, provided vendor readiness and safety-net implementation support are addressed.
- **S2/S3:** NOHN asks CMS to synchronize IG timelines and coordinate with ONC certification deadlines to avoid payer APIs going live before provider systems are ready.
- **S12:** NOHN identifies operational and technical challenges for drug ePA, including EHR/PMS/API integration, vendor readiness, cybersecurity, and limited CHC IT capacity.
- **S15:** NOHN directly asks CMS to clarify medical versus pharmacy benefit classification and whether one pathway's PA approval applies to the other.
- **S16/S17:** NOHN supports specific, actionable denial reasons for all drug PA denials and reporting on incomplete or unclear denial notices.
- **S18/S37:** NOHN supports ePA and required implementation standards but warns that CHCs need vendor accountability, testing, technical assistance, and funding.
- **S20/S43:** NOHN supports aligned and expedited PA decision timelines and asks CMS to impose automatic approval when required timeframes are missed.
- **S21:** NOHN supports drug ePA timelines but asks CMS to account for CHC readiness, payer rollout consistency, and provider technology availability.
- **S23-S27:** NOHN supports centralized, machine-readable API endpoint publication, 60-day initial reporting, one-week updates after changes, and annual verification.
- **S29/S30/S34/S35:** NOHN supports granular API usage metrics and recommends additional functionality, usability, error, workflow, and cost metrics; it also supports CMS publication of trends.
- **S44-S55:** NOHN supports FHIR as the direction for HIPAA PA standards but requests X12/FHIR transition support, CDex guardrails, enforcement discretion, and attention to small safety-net provider burden.
- **S60-S65:** NOHN asks CMS and ONC to harmonize standards and certification timing, assess HTI-5 impacts, and prevent certified technology gaps from disadvantaging CHCs.
- **S66-S82:** NOHN raises broader PA reform recommendations, including gold-carding for prescription drugs, sunset provisions for high-approval PA categories, and federal funding support for safety-net providers.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize interoperability and drug ePA requirements with realistic timelines and implementation support for CHCs.
2. Hold vendors, clearinghouses, and EHR systems accountable for readiness and clarify providers will not be penalized for failures outside their control.
3. Coordinate timelines with ONC certification and establish readiness validation/testing before enforcement.
4. Provide cybersecurity, IT workforce, technical assistance, and dedicated health IT funding for CHCs.
5. Require benefit classification information through Provider Access APIs using the CRD Coverage Information extension.
6. Clarify PA treatment for drugs covered under both medical and pharmacy benefits.
7. Coordinate with OPA on 340B-related pharmacy implementation issues.
8. Mandate proactive FHIR-based PA expiration alerts.
9. Pair ePA mandates with PA reduction, prescription drug gold-carding, and sunset provisions for high-approval PA categories.
10. Finalize faster and aligned PA decision timeframes and require specific, actionable denial reasons.
11. Establish automatic approval for PA requests not decided within required timeframes.
12. Publish PA metrics centrally on CMS's website and expand metrics to include service/medication category, first-pass approval, incomplete or unclear denial notices, data quality, and API functionality.
13. Publish API endpoints in centralized machine-readable files with timely updates.
14. Retain drug formulary information in Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs.
15. Extend HIPAA enforcement discretion for FHIR PA API use during the transition from X12.
16. Add CDex guardrails limiting iterative attachment requests.
17. Publish a CMS-ONC harmonization assessment before the final rule.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** CHC resource constraints, vendor readiness, cybersecurity exposure, fragmented payer requirements, dual medical/pharmacy workflows, pharmacy and 340B interoperability gaps, insufficient formulary visibility, PA delays, and certification timing mismatches.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Delayed medications, interrupted treatment, worsened chronic disease, abandoned care, increased administrative burden, noncompliance risk for providers acting in good faith, and disproportionate harm to rural and medically underserved patients.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Small IT teams, constrained budgets, EHR and third-party vendor dependence, pharmacy software/EHR/CoverMyMeds disconnects, limited interoperability in pharmacy systems, hard-coded endpoint disruptions, payer rollout variation, X12/FHIR dual-standard burden, and EHR certification gaps.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** AMA survey: 94% of physicians report PA delays patient care; patient surveys show average PA wait about three days and nearly one-third wait more than one week. KFF: MA organizations made nearly 53 million PA determinations in 2024 with more than four million full or partial denials. CHCs serve more than 16 million Medicaid beneficiaries, over 6 million uninsured individuals, 20.5 million low-income individuals, 1.1 million agricultural workers, and over 1.5 million homeless individuals; more than 90% of CHC patients have incomes below 200% FPL. NOHN receives about 100 PA requests daily and reports a case requiring over four physician hours, over 20 staff hours, and a three-month delay. Proactive expiration outreach is cited as positive in 87% of cases versus 25% without notification.
- **Studies or research referenced:** AMA, KFF, MGMA, HRSA UDS, NACHC, Pharmacy Times, Krauss et al., Murthi et al., Vishwanath et al., Lauffenburger et al., Salzbrenner et al., Fierce Healthcare, CMS enforcement discretion guidance, and WISeR model references.
- **Examples provided:** Extended-release buprenorphine may fall under pharmacy or medical benefit depending on dispensing/administration; NOHN names GLP-1s, buprenorphine, Adderall, Dexcom supplies, lidocaine patches, 340B contract pharmacy workflows, and an autoimmune lung disease/inflammatory arthritis infusion delayed three months.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** CHCs, rural safety-net providers, Medicaid/CHIP and low-income patients, homeless and agricultural worker populations, patients with chronic disease and behavioral health needs, payer organizations, pharmacy teams, 340B contract pharmacies, EHR and PMS vendors, clearinghouses, PBMs, app developers, ONC, OPA, and CMS.
- **Economic implications:** NOHN emphasizes unfunded IT, cybersecurity, vendor, API integration, staff training, pharmacy workflow, and PA labor costs; it notes CHCs operate on thin margins and many have limited cash on hand.
- **Technical feasibility:** NOHN supports FHIR/API modernization but views feasibility as dependent on vendor readiness, ONC certification timing, system interoperability, testing, funding, and coordinated standards.
- **Patient care impact:** If implemented with safeguards, the rule could improve medication access, adherence, continuity of care, prescribing decisions, care coordination, and accountability; without safeguards, it could increase burden and delay care for underserved patients.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with significant implementation modifications.
- **Tone:** Professional, urgent, practical, and safety-net focused.
- **Priority level:** High.

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Our small IT department and Pharmacy team cannot handle the current workload on PAs." - Context: CHC resource constraints.
2. "NOHN supports CMS' proposal to establish ePA requirements for prescription drugs." - Context: Core position on drug ePA.
3. "Electronic prior authorization alone may not reduce overall administrative burden" without PA reform. - Context: Request for gold-carding and sunset provisions.
4. "NOHN supports CMS' proposal to require impacted payers to report API endpoints" centrally. - Context: Support for endpoint reporting.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - NOHN focuses on October 1, 2027 deadlines, ONC certification gaps, X12/FHIR transition periods, and enforcement timing.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - The comment stresses limited CHC margins, small IT teams, cybersecurity costs, vendor upgrades, pharmacy integration, and unfunded PA labor.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - NOHN describes daily PA volume, staff burden, manual endpoint lookup, documentation burden, and iterative attachment requests.
- [x] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - The comment flags increased cybersecurity exposure from expanded API exchange involving sensitive patient information.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - NOHN emphasizes medically underserved, rural, low-income, homeless, agricultural worker, Medicaid, uninsured, and CHC patient impacts.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Vendor readiness, API consistency, pharmacy/EHR integration, certification timing, and testing are central feasibility concerns.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - NOHN discusses FHIR, CRD/DTR/PAS v2.2, CDex, X12 278/6020 coexistence, and ONC standards harmonization.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - The comment repeatedly links PA delays to medication access, chronic disease management, and treatment interruptions.
- [x] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - NOHN asks CMS to extend enforcement discretion, impose automatic approval, require reporting, and coordinate with ONC/OPA.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - The comment calls for CMS, ONC, OPA, vendors, clearinghouses, payers, EHRs, pharmacies, and CHCs to align.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - NOHN directly requests benefit classification transparency and cross-pathway PA clarification.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - NOHN supports denial reasons, CMS-published metrics, endpoint publication, formulary visibility, and PA status access.
- [x] **SMALL-PAYER-IMPACT** - The resource-constrained impact is framed around small safety-net providers rather than payers, but the comment is strongly focused on small-organization capacity.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - NOHN discusses current PA workflows, pharmacy operations, EHR/PMS disconnects, 340B workflows, X12, and CDex attachments.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Vendor readiness, EHR/PMS systems, clearinghouses, app developers, PBMs, and third-party platforms are major implementation concerns.
